The state machine then transitions through `PendingActivation → Enrolling → Running`. There is no "remote wake-up" mechanism — the agent in `Suspended` has no active timers, no network loops, and no way to detect that the portal has reactivated the host. "Portal reactivation" alone is insufficient because the agent has stopped listening. --- ## Enrollment trust model A stolen `activation.json` must **not** be enough to obtain a valid certificate on its own. This section defines the additional factors that pin a bundle to the specific host the admin intended. ### Threat model An attacker who obtains a freshly issued bundle (by intercepting a download, exfiltrating it from a share, etc.) could otherwise: 1. Run `reproduce-*` on an attacker-controlled machine. 2. Use the EAB credential and responder HMAC from the bundle to complete ACME enrollment. 3. Receive a valid short-lived certificate. 4. Connect to Giganto and masquerade as the intended host. The bundle's 1-hour TTL shrinks the race window but does not close it. An attacker who is fast enough, or who intercepts the bundle before the legitimate installer runs, can win the race. First-use binding (`E3`) catches the loser after the fact, but by then the attacker already holds a valid identity. ### Defense: portal-pinned host identity The portal requires an **admin-supplied host pre-registration** before issuing a bundle. At least one of the following two paths must be used; both are acceptable for v1, and the portal records which path was chosen for audit. **Path A — MDM-sourced pre-registration (preferred where MDM is in place)** 1. The admin selects the target host from an MDM inventory (Intune, Jamf, Kandji, etc.) inside the portal's "Add host" flow. 2. The portal reads the MDM-provided host identifier: Windows `MachineGuid`, Linux `/etc/machine-id`, or macOS `IOPlatformUUID`. 3. The portal records the value in `host.expected_fingerprint` and binds it to the activation token. 4. The bundle and MSI/pkg/.deb are delivered to the host through the MDM channel, not as a user download. 5. On first enrollment the agent reads the same local identifier and embeds it in the CSR through a custom extension (see "Wire format" below). The authorizing webhook extracts the value and compares it to `host.expected_fingerprint`. A mismatch returns `{"allow": false, "reason": "fingerprint_mismatch"}`. **Important caveat about Path A's strength.** `MachineGuid`, `/etc/machine-id`, and `IOPlatformUUID` are *readable values*, not *cryptographic attestations*. Any process running on the host can read them, and an attacker who at any point had access to the victim host (or to a backup or an inventory dump) can reproduce them. Path A therefore **raises the bar significantly** — an attacker must obtain both the bundle *and* the victim's fingerprint, two values that travel through completely different channels — but it is **not** the same as TPM-rooted device identity. Hardware-rooted attestation via `device-attest-01` + TPM (Windows / Linux) and Secure Enclave (macOS) is tracked as a v2 candidate. **Path B — portal-issued one-time nonce (for sites without MDM)** 1. The admin clicks "Add host" and provides the target hostname and a short description. 2. The portal generates two values: the normal activation bundle **and a short 8-character nonce** displayed only to the admin in the UI. 3. The admin delivers the bundle *and the nonce* to the host via two separate channels (e.g. the bundle via file copy, the nonce via phone, chat, or SMS to the installing operator). 4. The installer prompts for the nonce alongside the bundle path. The agent embeds the nonce in the CSR through a custom extension (see "Wire format" below). 5. The authorizing webhook extracts the nonce and verifies it against `host.expected_nonce_hash` (constant-time comparison against a stored hash). The nonce is single-use and consumed on first successful enrollment. This path requires a live out-of-band channel (phone, chat) but does not require MDM. It reduces the attack surface from "whoever can read the bundle file" to "whoever can read the bundle file AND intercepts the out-of-band nonce". ### Wire format — how the second factor reaches the webhook step-ca's authorizing webhook receives the parsed CSR as JSON. The agent's second-factor value therefore has to live **inside the CSR itself**. We carry it in **custom X.509 extensions under a private OID arc** so that the values are visible to the webhook but can be stripped from the issued certificate by the step-ca template (we do not want fingerprints or nonces baked into long-lived public artifacts). Two private OIDs under the organization's IANA Private Enterprise Number (PEN) are reserved: | OID (placeholder, exact PEN to be assigned in `reproduce/specs/activation-bundle.md`) | Name | Value | Used by | |---|---|---|---| | `1.3.6.1.4.1..1.1` | `reproduceHostFingerprint` | UTF-8 string, hex-encoded fingerprint of the host (Windows `MachineGuid`, Linux `/etc/machine-id`, or macOS `IOPlatformUUID`) | **Both Path A and Path B** | | `1.3.6.1.4.1..1.2` | `reproduceEnrollmentNonce` | UTF-8 string, the 8-character one-time nonce | **Path B only** | The agent **always** includes its local host fingerprint in the CSR (OID `.1.1`). For Path B, the nonce (OID `.1.2`) is also included. The difference is how the portal uses each value: | OID | Path A | Path B | |---|---|---| | `reproduceHostFingerprint` (.1.1) | **Authentication factor** (Phase 1): webhook compares to `host.expected_fingerprint`; mismatch → deny. **Forensic record** (Phase 2): the value is written to `host.observed_fingerprint` (set-once) when Giganto confirms the first connection | **Verification skipped** (Phase 1): `host.expected_fingerprint` is null, so no comparison. **Forensic record** (Phase 2): same as Path A — `observed_fingerprint` is set-once on confirmation | | `reproduceEnrollmentNonce` (.1.2) | Not present in CSR | **Authentication factor** (Phase 1): webhook hashes and compares to `host.expected_nonce_hash` (constant-time, KDF); mismatch → deny. **Consumed** (Phase 2): `expected_nonce_hash` is cleared when Giganto confirms the first connection, not at webhook time | Agent side: - The ACME client (`instant-acme` plus a small wrapper in `src/enrollment/acme.rs`) always reads the local host fingerprint and writes it into the CSR as OID `.1.1`, regardless of which trust path is configured. - For Path A, this is all that is needed — the fingerprint is the second factor. - For Path B, the agent additionally prompts the installer for the nonce and writes it into the CSR as OID `.1.2`. The nonce is then discarded from memory. step-ca side: - The `endpoints` provisioner template **explicitly drops** both extensions before signing — they exist only to be read by the webhook and are not present in the issued cert. - step-ca passes the parsed CSR (including the extensions) to the webhook in its standard `x509CertificateRequest` payload. Portal side (`POST /api/authz/host`, authenticated by mTLS + HMAC): - Extract both extensions from the CSR by OID. OID `.1.1` (fingerprint) is always present; OID `.1.2` (nonce) is present only for Path B. - **Fingerprint verification** (both paths): For Path A, compare the extracted fingerprint to `host.expected_fingerprint` in constant time — a mismatch returns `{"allow": false, "reason": "fingerprint_mismatch"}`. For Path B, `host.expected_fingerprint` is null, so no comparison is performed. - **Nonce verification** (Path B only): hash the extracted nonce with the same KDF used to populate `host.expected_nonce_hash` and compare in constant time. A mismatch returns `{"allow": false, "reason": "nonce_mismatch"}`. - **Retry-safe logic** (Path B, handles the "allowed but cert never received" edge case): if `host.expected_nonce_hash` is already null (consumed by a prior Phase 2 confirmation) but `host.cert_serial` is still null (no confirmation has arrived yet), this would indicate an inconsistent state — in the two-phase model nonce consumption and cert_serial are set atomically in Phase 2, so this combination should not occur. If `host.expected_nonce_hash` is **not** null (normal case for a first or retried enrollment), the nonce is verified normally. If `host.status` is `Enrolling` and `host.cert_serial` is null (Phase 2 has not yet fired), a retried finalize simply re-runs the same verification — the nonce is still available because Phase 1 does not consume it. See "Enrollment lifecycle: two-phase confirmation" below. - If all checks pass, return `{"allow": true}`. **No permanent state mutations happen at this point.** The webhook is a pure authorization check; the one-time credentials (nonce, observed_fingerprint) are consumed only after enrollment is confirmed. See below. ### Enrollment lifecycle: two-phase confirmation A critical subtlety: **webhook `{"allow": true}` does not mean "the agent has a cert in hand"**. Between the webhook response and the agent's successful cert installation, the following steps can still fail: ``` webhook allow → step-ca signs cert → agent downloads cert → agent stores locally → agent connects to Giganto ↑ can fail (network) ↑ can fail (disk) ``` If `observed_fingerprint` were recorded and the nonce consumed at webhook time, a download failure would leave the enrollment in a broken state: the one-time credentials are gone but the agent never received its cert. This would lock out Path B enrollments. The design therefore uses a **two-phase model**: **Phase 1 — Authorization + scoped enrollment lease (webhook time)** The webhook checks fingerprint, nonce, and host authorization status. **Lease behavior depends on the host's current state:** *Initial enrollment (`host.status = Enrolling`):* If all checks pass and no lease is currently held, the webhook sets a **scoped enrollment lease** on the host row: - `host.pending_issuance_key_hash = SHA-256(CSR public key)` — the lease is bound to a specific CSR key, not to the host as a whole. - `host.pending_since = now()` Subsequent webhook calls for the **same host** are handled as follows: | Subsequent call's CSR key hash | Lease status | Decision | |---|---|---| | Matches `pending_issuance_key_hash` | Lease held | **Allow** (idempotent retry — the agent is re-trying its own enrollment) | | Does not match | Lease held | **Deny** (`enrollment_already_in_progress` — a different key means a different ACME flow, which is the concurrent-issuance attack the lease prevents) | | Any | Lease expired | **Allow** (lease timed out; treat as a fresh attempt, re-set the lease with the new key hash) | The lease timeout is set to the **ACME order lifetime** configured in step-ca (typically 1–4 hours), not the cert lifetime (24 hours). This ensures that a failed first attempt does not block retries for longer than the order would have been valid anyway. *Renewal (`host.status = Active`):* **No enrollment lease is set or checked.** Renewals are a fundamentally different flow: the host already has a confirmed `cert_serial`, and the ACME account already exists. A duplicate renewal cert is a minor concern (two valid certs briefly overlap until the old one expires) and is far less dangerous than a service outage caused by a lease blocking a legitimate retry during the 8-hour renewal window. If a renewal webhook fails after `allow`, the agent simply retries the ACME order or cert download with backoff. Nonce verification is not involved in renewals — `expected_nonce_hash` was already consumed during the original Phase 2 confirmation and is null for any host in `Active` status. Other than the lease fields, the webhook does **not** mutate permanent host state. `observed_fingerprint`, `expected_nonce_hash`, `activation_token.used_at`, and `host.status` all remain unchanged until Phase 2. **Phase 2 — Confirmation (first Giganto connection)** When the agent connects to Giganto for the first time with its newly issued cert, Giganto observes a cert serial that is not yet recorded. Giganto exposes this as a **GraphQL subscription** event (`sensorConnected`). The portal subscribes to this subscription over the existing mTLS-authenticated GraphQL connection and receives a notification with `{ agent_name, cert_serial }`. On receiving the event, the portal atomically: 1. Sets `host.cert_serial` to the confirmed serial. 2. Sets `host.observed_fingerprint` to the fingerprint extracted during the most recent webhook call (**set-once**, only if null). 3. Clears `host.expected_nonce_hash` (Path B nonce consumed). 4. Marks `activation_token.used_at`. 5. Clears `host.pending_issuance_key_hash` and `host.pending_since` (enrollment lease released). 6. Transitions `host.status` from `Enrolling` to `Active`. 7. Logs an `enrollment.confirmed` audit event. Until Phase 2 fires, the host stays in `Enrolling` and all one-time credentials remain valid. However, the **pending enrollment lease** set in Phase 1 prevents a second concurrent ACME flow from a different key — only one issuance can be in flight at a time (idempotent retries with the same key are allowed). If the first attempt fails entirely (agent crashes, order expires, etc.), the lease times out after the **ACME order lifetime** (typically 1–4 hours), releasing the host for a fresh attempt. **Edge cases:** | Scenario | What happens | |---|---| | Webhook allows, agent downloads cert, connects to Giganto normally | Phase 2 fires within seconds. Normal path. | | Webhook allows, step-ca signs, but agent can't download (network error) | Agent retries ACME cert download (order stays valid). Lease is held but a retry with the same CSR key passes through (idempotent). No permanent state changed. | | Webhook allows, agent downloads, but can't store locally (disk error) | Agent retries storage. Lease is held. No permanent state changed. | | Webhook allows, but ACME order expires before agent downloads | Agent creates a new order with the same key pair, re-finalizes. Webhook fires again → CSR key hash matches the lease → **allowed** (idempotent retry). If the agent generates a new key pair, the hash won't match, but if the lease has timed out (ACME order lifetime, 1–4h), a fresh lease is granted. | | Agent crashes or is uninstalled after webhook allow, before Phase 2 | Lease times out after the ACME order lifetime (1–4h), then the host returns to a clean `Enrolling` state. Admin can also manually clear the lease and reissue the bundle. | | Attacker tries to use the same bundle on a different machine while the legitimate agent is enrolling | Attacker's CSR uses a different key pair → key hash does not match → lease blocks with `enrollment_already_in_progress`. | | Renewal fails after webhook allow (agent can't download new cert) | No lease was set (renewals skip the lease). Agent retries with backoff against the same step-ca order or a new one. Existing cert remains valid for the remaining 8 hours. | | Webhook allows, agent gets cert, but Giganto is unreachable | Agent stays in `Enrolling`. When Giganto becomes reachable, Phase 2 fires. Cert is valid for 24h, so there is a time limit. | | Phase 2 never fires within cert lifetime (24h) | Host stays `Enrolling`. Admin can investigate and reissue the bundle if needed. | **Giganto-side implementation:** Giganto already tracks connected sensors internally (`ingest_sensors` in `comm/ingest.rs`). For Phase 2 confirmation, Giganto adds a **GraphQL subscription** that streams new-sensor-connection events: ```graphql type Subscription { sensorConnected: SensorConnectionEvent! } type SensorConnectionEvent { agentName: String! certSerial: String! timestamp: DateTime! } ``` - On each new QUIC ingest connection, after SAN verification and deny-list check, Giganto checks whether the cert serial has been seen before for this `agent_name`. - If the serial is new, Giganto publishes a `SensorConnectionEvent` to the subscription. - The portal subscribes to `sensorConnected` over the existing mTLS-authenticated GraphQL WebSocket connection (the same `graphql_srv_addr` endpoint already used for queries and mutations). No new outbound HTTP client is needed in Giganto — the portal initiates and maintains the subscription connection. - If the portal is temporarily disconnected, events are missed but the portal can recover by querying the current sensor list (a new `connectedSensors` query) on reconnection and comparing against its host table. This approach requires **no new outbound networking in Giganto** — it only adds a subscription and mutations to the existing GraphQL schema. The portal establishes a **new** mTLS WebSocket connection to Giganto's GraphQL endpoint (see "Implementation note — new outbound connections" above) and subscribes. Neither portal currently connects to Giganto directly, so this is new infrastructure on the portal side. The subscription event schema is defined in **`giganto/specs/enrollment-confirmation.md`**. The portal-side subscription handler is defined in **`aice-web-next/specs/enrollment-confirmation.md`** (and the equivalent file in `aimer-web`). The exact OID values, the encoding of the extension content, and the JSON shape of the webhook payload are defined in **`reproduce/specs/activation-bundle.md`** and **`aice-web-next/specs/authz-webhook.md`** (and the equivalent file in `aimer-web`). Those spec files are the canonical source for implementation; the description here is for design rationale. ### Two distinct fingerprint values Avoid conflating these: | Column | Set when | Set by | Purpose | Affects issuance? | |---|---|---|---|---| | `host.expected_fingerprint` | Before bundle issuance (Path A only) | Admin (via MDM lookup in the portal UI) | Authentication factor — the webhook compares the agent's submitted value to this | **Yes**: a mismatch returns `{"allow": false, "reason": "fingerprint_mismatch"}` | | `host.observed_fingerprint` | On enrollment confirmation (Phase 2, **set-once**, both Paths) | Agent fingerprint extracted from the most recent webhook call, recorded when Giganto confirms first connection | Forensic baseline — "which physical machine originally enrolled with this identity?" | **No**: it is a post-confirmation record and is never overwritten | `observed_fingerprint` is **immutable once set**. On subsequent renewals the agent still includes its current fingerprint in the CSR (OID `.1.1`), but the webhook does not overwrite `observed_fingerprint`; instead it logs the value as an `enrollment.renewal_fingerprint` audit event. This preserves the original forensic record while still providing an ongoing trail of which machine is currently renewing. If the renewal fingerprint ever differs from `observed_fingerprint`, the admin can investigate whether the host was reimaged, the bundle was sideloaded onto a different machine, or the identity was compromised. ### Bundle TTL and re-download policy — tightened To limit the race window further: - TTL is reduced to **15 minutes** (down from 1 hour) for the bundle itself. - Re-download is **disabled by default**. If the admin needs to re-download, they must explicitly click "Reissue bundle", which generates a new EAB, new responder HMAC kid, and a new nonce (Path B) or re-reads the MDM fingerprint (Path A). - A bundle that has been re-downloaded once is marked `superseded` and cannot be used even if the original file still exists somewhere. ### Bundle contents — factor separation `activation.json` intentionally does **not** contain the MDM fingerprint (Path A) or the nonce (Path B). Those are held by the host's hardware or the admin's out-of-band channel. This makes the bundle useless on its own even if intercepted. ### Summary | Factor | Held by | How it is delivered to the agent | How the portal verifies | |---|---|---|---| | EAB credential | activation bundle | bundle file | step-ca consumes on `newAccount` | | Responder HMAC | activation bundle | bundle file | bootroot responder verifies | | Host fingerprint (Path A) | host hardware | read locally by the agent | authorizing webhook compares to `host.expected_fingerprint` | | One-time nonce (Path B) | admin, out-of-band | admin enters during installation | authorizing webhook hashes and compares to `host.expected_nonce_hash` (constant-time, KDF), single-use | A single stolen factor cannot produce a valid cert. Both the bundle **and** either a matching hardware identifier or an intercepted out-of-band nonce are required. --- ## Activation bundle `activation.json` ### Schema ```json { "version": "1", "issued_at": "2026-04-11T14:30:00Z", "expires_at": "2026-04-11T14:45:00Z", "host_id": "01HP5NXQ...", "san_identifier": "01HP5NXQ.endpoints.aimer.aicers.com", "agent_name": "01HP5NXQ", "kind": "sysmon", "grant_scope": { "kind": "environment_customer", "aice_id": "env-prod-kr", "customer_id": "cust-division-a" }, "trust_model": { "second_factor": "mdm_fingerprint" }, "step_ca": { "directory": "https://step-ca.endpoints.aimer.aicers.com/acme/endpoints/directory", "ca_root_pem": "-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----\n..." }, "eab": { "kid": "eab_01HP5...", "hmac_b64": "..." }, "responder": { "url": "https://responder.endpoints.aimer.aicers.com", "hmac_kid": "hmac_01HP5...", "hmac_secret_b64": "..." }, "giganto": { "addr": "giganto.aimer.aicers.com:38370", "server_name": "giganto.aimer.aicers.com" } } ``` Note: `trust_model.second_factor` tells the agent which second factor to collect at enrollment time. `"mdm_fingerprint"` = Path A (read local hardware ID), `"nonce"` = Path B (prompt the installing admin). The bundle never contains the actual fingerprint or nonce value. ### Delivery and lifetime - Downloadable only through an authenticated portal session. - TTL of **15 minutes** from issuance. A bundle past its TTL is unusable even if copied elsewhere. - **Re-download is disabled by default.** If the admin needs another copy, they must explicitly click "Reissue bundle", which invalidates the previous bundle and all its credentials (new EAB, new responder HMAC kid, new nonce or re-read MDM fingerprint). - Once the bundle is used for a successful enrollment, the portal marks it as consumed and it cannot be reused. - The agent also deletes the file after a successful enrollment to prevent reuse. - MDM-based deployment: Windows via an MSI property that specifies a **file path** (e.g. `BUNDLE_PATH=C:\path\to\activation.json`), **never the bundle content itself** — command-line arguments appear in Windows Installer logs, Sysmon `ProcessCreate` events, and MDM deployment logs, so passing the raw JSON (which contains EAB and HMAC secrets) on the command line would expose them. Linux via a file placed at `/etc/reproduce/activation.json`. macOS via the pkg payload. In all MDM scenarios, Path A of the enrollment trust model is strongly recommended so that the bundle and the host fingerprint are never in the same channel. ### Security properties - The EAB credential and the responder HMAC are **two distinct credentials** with separate signing contexts, so a compromise of one does not breach the other. - The responder HMAC is **scoped per host**, so it cannot register tokens for any identifier other than the one assigned to that host. - The EAB credential is single-use. After the first ACME `newAccount` call, step-ca retires it. - The bundle **does not contain the second factor** (neither the MDM fingerprint nor the out-of-band nonce). A leaked bundle on its own cannot complete enrollment. See "Enrollment trust model" above. --- ## Enrollment and renewal flow ### First enrollment (sequence) ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant A as reproduce-* participant R as responder participant C as step-ca participant P as portal participant G as Giganto Note over A: startup: parse bundle,
generate key pair A->>C: ① newAccount + EAB A->>C: ② newOrder (identifier: host-id.endpoints.) C-->>A: HTTP-01 challenge + token A->>R: ③ POST /admin/http01
(token + keyAuth, signed with X-Kid) Note over R: scope validation,
store token A->>C: ④ trigger challenge C->>R: GET /.well-known/acme-challenge/token R-->>C: keyAuth A->>C: ⑤ finalize(CSR) C->>P: authorizing webhook (mTLS + HMAC)
POST /api/authz/host P-->>C: {"allow": true} C-->>A: cert + chain Note over A: KeyStore.store(identity),
delete activation.json A->>G: ⑥ connect (mTLS with issued cert) Note over G: verify SAN ↔ agent_name,
check deny list A->>G: event stream starts ``` ### Renewal (at 2/3 of the cert lifetime) - The agent reuses the existing ACME account key to create a new order. - It registers the HTTP-01 challenge token with the responder under the per-host HMAC kid distributed at enrollment. The responder HMAC is not rotated on renewal. - After the challenge succeeds, the agent submits `finalize`. - **Before signing, step-ca calls the portal's authorizing webhook** (see "Authorization webhook" below) to re-check whether the host is still authorized. The webhook receives the requested identifier and returns `{"allow": true}` or `{"allow": false, "reason": "..."}`. - If the webhook allows, step-ca issues the new cert, the agent fetches it, and `KeyStore::rotate()` performs an atomic swap. - If the webhook denies, step-ca rejects the finalize step with an ACME error. The agent receives `EnrollmentError::Denied` and stays in `Running` for as long as the existing cert is still valid. ### Authorization webhook — how step-ca asks the portal The portal is the authoritative source for host authorization; step-ca itself has no knowledge of which hosts are still allowed. The link between the two is a **step-ca `AUTHORIZING` webhook** configured on the `endpoints` provisioner. Flow on every issuance (initial enrollment and every renewal): ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant A as agent participant C as step-ca participant P as portal A->>C: finalize(CSR, identifier = host-id.endpoints.) Note over C: before signing,
step-ca calls the webhook C->>P: POST /api/authz/host (over mTLS)
X-Smallstep-Signature: HMAC(body)
{ "request": { "identifier": ..., "san": [...], "extensions": [...] } } Note over P: look up host authorization state:
• host.status in {Enrolling, Active}?
• customer / environment within expiry?
• still inside max_hosts? alt host still authorized P-->>C: {"allow": true} C-->>A: new cert + chain else host suspended or revoked P-->>C: {"allow": false, "reason": "host_suspended"} C-->>A: ACME error
(EnrollmentError::Denied on the agent side) end ``` Key properties of the webhook: - **Defense in depth: HMAC plus mTLS**. Step-ca signs every webhook request with a shared secret stored in OpenBao, and the underlying HTTPS transport uses **mTLS between step-ca and the portal** (step-ca presents the certificate issued by its own internal-services provisioner; the portal pins that certificate's issuer). HMAC alone would suffice for authentication, but combining it with mTLS localizes the trust surface: even if the HMAC secret leaks, an attacker still needs a valid client certificate from the internal services CA to reach the endpoint at all. The portal rejects any call that fails either check. - **Stateless from step-ca's side**: step-ca keeps no host allow/deny list of its own. Every decision goes back to the portal, which is the single source of truth. - **Immediate effect**: once the admin flips `host.status` in the portal database, the next webhook invocation (i.e. the next renewal attempt for that host) sees the change. There is no cache or replication delay. - **Audit trail**: every webhook call is logged on both sides — step-ca records the decision, and the portal records who asked (mTLS client identity + HMAC kid), the host identifier, and the decision returned. - **Logging redaction of secret material**: the CSR body contains the host fingerprint (OID `.1.1`) and potentially the enrollment nonce (OID `.1.2`). These are security-sensitive values — the nonce is a one-time credential, and the fingerprint is a stable device identifier that may constitute personal data. **Neither step-ca nor the portal may log the raw CSR body or the raw extension values.** Audit log entries for webhook calls must record only: (a) the host identifier (SAN), (b) a truncated SHA-256 hash of the fingerprint value (first 8 hex characters), (c) `nonce_present: true/false` (never the nonce itself), (d) the decision (`allow`/`deny` + reason). This constraint is explicitly called out in `reproduce/specs/activation-bundle.md` and `aice-web-next/specs/authz-webhook.md` as a MUST-level requirement. step-ca's own logging configuration must also be reviewed to ensure that CSR bodies are not emitted at `info` or `debug` log levels in production deployments. ### Suspension / blocking (two-layer defense: server-side block + agent self-suspension) ```mermaid sequenceDiagram actor Admin participant P as portal participant G as Giganto participant A as reproduce-host-abc participant C as step-ca Admin->>P: click "suspend host-abc" P->>P: host.status = Suspended P->>G: GraphQL mutation addDenyListEntry
{ certSerial: "S", expiresAt: ... } Note over C: next renewal will be denied
via the authorizing webhook Note over G,A: Layer 1 — server-side block G->>G: add S to deny list (until cert NotAfter) G->>A: HOST_DENIED on active connection, then close Note over G: on every new connection attempt,
check cert serial against deny list,
send HOST_DENIED + close on match Note over A: Layer 2 — agent self-suspension A->>A: GigantoDenialReceived
(Running/Renewing → Suspended) A->>A: Collector stopped
(Sysmon / Falco / osquery) A->>A: Sender stopped
(no reconnect attempts) A->>A: Checkpoint preserved A->>A: log Suspended + reason Note over A: service stays alive in Suspended,
waiting for admin intervention ``` **Result:** - Within seconds of the admin click, the host fully stops sending data. - No new events accumulate locally, which prevents privacy and legal issues. - The agent enters a clean `Suspended` state instead of generating an endless retry-failure log. - step-ca denies the next renewal via the authorizing webhook, so the current cert retires naturally on expiry. ### The two layers | Layer | Implementation location | Purpose | Reaction time | |---|---|---|---| | **Layer 1** — deny list | Giganto server | Prevent unauthorized data from **reaching Giganto** | Seconds | | **Layer 2** — self-suspension | `reproduce-*` agent | Prevent the agent from **even attempting to collect or send** while unauthorized | Immediately upon receiving the Giganto denial | With Layer 1 alone, a still-running agent would enter an endless retry loop and waste local CPU, logs, and event queue space. With Layer 2 alone, a modified agent could bypass enforcement entirely. **Both layers are required.** ### Deny list management - Entries are kept only until the cert's NotAfter - Automatic removal after NotAfter (the cert is naturally invalid at that point, so there is no need to remember it) - Giganto keeps the list in memory with disk persistence (restored on restart) - Deny list management via Giganto's **GraphQL API** (mTLS-authenticated, same endpoint as existing queries/mutations): - `mutation addDenyListEntry(certSerial, expiresAt)` — add an entry - `mutation removeDenyListEntry(certSerial)` — remove early - `query denyList` — query the current list (for operations and audit) --- ## Portal design ### aice-web-next — host authorization extension **Schema additions** (in the existing `auth_db` or a new database) ```sql ALTER TABLE customer ADD COLUMN max_hosts INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0; ALTER TABLE customer ADD COLUMN host_auth_expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ; CREATE TABLE host ( id UUID PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customer(id), agent_id TEXT NOT NULL, san_identifier TEXT NOT NULL, status TEXT NOT NULL, -- Pending | Enrolling | Active | Suspended | Revoked trust_path TEXT NOT NULL, -- 'mdm_fingerprint' or 'nonce' expected_fingerprint TEXT, -- set for trust_path = 'mdm_fingerprint' expected_nonce_hash TEXT, -- bcrypt/argon2 hash for trust_path = 'nonce' observed_fingerprint TEXT, -- set-once on Phase 2 confirmation, for drift detection pending_issuance_key_hash TEXT, -- SHA-256 of CSR public key; set on webhook allow (Enrolling only), cleared by Phase 2 or ACME-order-lifetime timeout pending_since TIMESTAMPTZ, -- when the lease was set cert_serial TEXT, enrolled_at TIMESTAMPTZ, last_renewed_at TIMESTAMPTZ, last_seen_at TIMESTAMPTZ, created_by UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES account(id), created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now() ); CREATE TABLE activation_token ( id UUID PRIMARY KEY, host_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES host(id), eab_kid TEXT NOT NULL, responder_hmac_kid TEXT NOT NULL, issued_by UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES account(id), issued_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL, expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL, used_at TIMESTAMPTZ ); ``` **Authorization validation rule** (on host creation) ``` valid := customer.status = 'Active' ∧ customer.host_auth_expires_at > now() ∧ count(host where customer_id = C) < customer.max_hosts ``` **New API endpoints** - `POST /api/hosts` — create a host (validate authorization, create host and activation_token rows, register EAB and responder HMAC with step-ca and bootroot, return the `activation.json`) - `GET /api/hosts` — list hosts (customer-scoped) - `DELETE /api/hosts/{id}` — suspend/revoke (update host.status, push to Giganto deny list; the next renewal is automatically denied via the authorization webhook below) - `POST /api/hosts/{id}/renew-bundle` — reissue the activation bundle when the previous one expired - **Giganto `sensorConnected` subscription handler** — The portal subscribes to Giganto's `sensorConnected` GraphQL subscription over the existing mTLS connection. When a `SensorConnectionEvent { agentName, certSerial }` arrives for a host in `Enrolling` status, the handler triggers Phase 2: atomically sets `host.cert_serial`, `host.observed_fingerprint` (set-once), clears `host.expected_nonce_hash` (Path B), marks `activation_token.used_at`, clears the pending enrollment lease, and transitions `host.status` to `Active`. Idempotent — duplicate events for the same serial are no-ops. On reconnection after a subscription drop, the portal queries `connectedSensors` to catch any events missed during the gap. - `POST /api/authz/host` — **step-ca authorization webhook target.** Called by step-ca over an **mTLS connection** (step-ca presents its internal-services client certificate; the portal pins the issuer) before every certificate issuance. The portal verifies both the mTLS peer identity **and** the HMAC signature (`X-Smallstep-Signature` header) before processing the request. It then looks up the host in the `host` table, checks customer status and `max_hosts`, verifies the second-factor CSR extension (fingerprint or nonce), and returns `{"allow": true}` or `{"allow": false, "reason": "..."}`. The shared HMAC secret is stored in OpenBao. This endpoint is not exposed to end users; it is reachable only by step-ca's mTLS identity. **New permissions** - `hosts:read` — list and detail views - `hosts:write` — add / suspend / revoke hosts Grantable to System Administrator and Tenant Administrator. Whether Security Monitor gets a read-only view is deferred. The `/api/authz/host` endpoint has no user-facing permission; it is authenticated by **mTLS peer identity plus HMAC signature** from step-ca, not by an account. **UI** — a new "Host management" page - Pick a customer → list of hosts (status, cert expiry, last connection timestamp) - "Add host" button → dialog → download `activation.json` + MSI/pkg/.deb - Row actions: "Suspend", "Revoke", "Reissue activation bundle" **Audit events** (on top of the existing audit_db schema) - `host.created` / `host.suspended` / `host.revoked` / `host.renewed` - `activation_token.issued` / `activation_token.used` / `activation_token.expired` - `enrollment.succeeded` / `enrollment.denied` / `enrollment.failed` - `enrollment.confirmed` — Phase 2 confirmation: Giganto reported the first connection with a new cert serial; `host.cert_serial`, `observed_fingerprint`, nonce consumption, and `status = Active` all committed atomically - `enrollment.renewal_fingerprint` — logged on every renewal when the agent's current fingerprint is received via the CSR; preserves the trail without overwriting the set-once `observed_fingerprint` - `authz_webhook.allowed` / `authz_webhook.denied` — every invocation of `/api/authz/host` from step-ca, including the host id, the decision, and the reason for denial ### aimer-web — two-tier allocation model Because a single customer in aimer-web can belong to multiple Environments, allocation is modelled in **two tiers**: an Environment-wide ceiling plus a per-(environment, customer) sub-allocation. **Schema additions / extensions** ```sql ALTER TABLE aice_environments ADD COLUMN max_hosts INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0; ALTER TABLE aice_environments ADD COLUMN host_auth_expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ; -- Note: aimer-web uses aice_id (TEXT) to identify environments and UUID for customer IDs. -- This differs from aice-web-next which uses INTEGER customer IDs. ALTER TABLE aice_environment_customers ADD COLUMN max_hosts INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0; ALTER TABLE aice_environment_customers ADD COLUMN host_auth_expires_at TIMESTAMPTZ; CREATE TABLE host ( id UUID PRIMARY KEY, aice_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES aice_environments(aice_id), customer_id UUID NOT NULL, agent_id TEXT NOT NULL, san_identifier TEXT NOT NULL, status TEXT NOT NULL, -- Pending | Enrolling | Active | Suspended | Revoked (same enum as aice-web-next) trust_path TEXT NOT NULL, expected_fingerprint TEXT, expected_nonce_hash TEXT, observed_fingerprint TEXT, pending_issuance_key_hash TEXT, pending_since TIMESTAMPTZ, cert_serial TEXT, enrolled_at TIMESTAMPTZ, last_renewed_at TIMESTAMPTZ, last_seen_at TIMESTAMPTZ, created_by UUID NOT NULL, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), FOREIGN KEY (aice_id, customer_id) REFERENCES aice_environment_customers(aice_id, customer_id) ); CREATE TABLE activation_token ( -- same shape as aice-web-next ); ``` **Authorization validation rule (two tiers)** ``` env_valid := aice_environments.status = 'active' ∧ aice_environments.host_auth_expires_at > now() ∧ count(host where aice_id = A) < aice_environments.max_hosts ec_valid := (aice_id, customer_id) mapping exists in aice_environment_customers ∧ aice_environment_customers.host_auth_expires_at > now() ∧ count(host where aice_id = A and customer_id = C) < aice_environment_customers.max_hosts valid := env_valid ∧ ec_valid ``` **Invariants on allocation editing** - The sum of per-customer sub-allocations may not exceed the Environment ceiling. - Lowering a limit below the current active host count is allowed; the excess hosts will expire naturally as their renewals are denied. **UI, API, and permissions** — structurally aligned with aice-web-next. Permissions introduce the new `hosts:read` and `hosts:write` alongside the existing `aice-environments:*`, granted to the same roles that manage Environments today. The same `POST /api/authz/host` authorization webhook endpoint is exposed here as well, authenticated by **mTLS plus HMAC** (identical to the aice-web-next contract). It reuses the two-tier validation rule above (Environment-wide ceiling plus per-(environment, customer) sub-allocation). ### Similarities and differences between the two portals | Axis | aice-web-next | aimer-web | |---|---|---| | Gate unit | customer (INTEGER id) | `aice_environments` + `aice_environment_customers` (two tiers) | | `host` table FK | `customer_id INTEGER` | `(aice_id TEXT, customer_id UUID)` | | Validation tiers | 1 | 2 | | Shared | `activation_token` schema, permission names, API contract, audit event types, UI skeleton | | The API contract (request and response format) is **deliberately identical** between the two portals, so that a `reproduce-*` client can run the same enrollment protocol against either portal. --- ## bootroot / step-ca extensions ### step-ca configuration — new `endpoints` provisioner Alongside the existing `internal-services` provisioner, add a new one: ```json { "type": "ACME", "name": "endpoints", "forceCN": true, "requireEAB": true, "challenges": ["http-01"], "claims": { "maxTLSCertDuration": "24h", "defaultTLSCertDuration": "24h", "minTLSCertDuration": "1h" }, "options": { "x509": { "templateData": { "sans": [...] // per-host identifier pattern policy } }, "webhooks": [ { "name": "portal-host-authorization", "kind": "AUTHORIZING", "url": "https:///api/authz/host", "secret": "" } ] } } ``` Two policies apply here: - **SAN template policy** — restricts the issued identifier to the `.endpoints.` pattern so that the provisioner cannot be tricked into issuing certificates for arbitrary names. - **Authorizing webhook** — on every issuance (initial enrollment and every renewal), step-ca calls the portal's `POST /api/authz/host` endpoint over **mTLS** and signs the request body with the shared HMAC secret. The portal verifies both the mTLS peer identity and the HMAC signature, then checks host authorization state. step-ca only signs the certificate if the portal responds `{"allow": true}`. See "Authorization webhook — how step-ca asks the portal" above for the full flow. ### bootroot-http01-responder extension — scoped HMAC mode Today the responder runs with a single master HMAC configured in `settings.acme.http_responder_hmac`. We extend it to support a **dual mode**: **Code changes** (bootroot repo) ```rust // existing fn verify_master_hmac(req, master_secret) { ... } // after the extension enum HmacMode { Master(Vec), Scoped(Box), } trait HmacStore: Send + Sync { fn get(&self, kid: &str) -> Option; } struct HmacEntry { secret: Vec, scope_pattern: String, // e.g. "host-abc.endpoints.aimer.aicers.com" expires_at: Option, } fn verify_request(req, mode) { if req.headers.contains("X-Kid") { // Scoped mode: kid lookup → scope check → HMAC verify let kid = req.headers["X-Kid"]; let entry = store.get(kid).ok_or(Unauthorized)?; if !matches_scope(&entry.scope_pattern, &req.body.identifier) { return Err(Forbidden); } verify_hmac(req, &entry.secret) } else { // Master mode: existing behavior verify_hmac(req, master_secret) } } ``` **OpenBao KV layout (new)** ``` secret/bootroot/http01-hmac (existing, internal-services master) secret/endpoints/http01-hmac-store/{kid} (new, per-host endpoint entries) ``` **Admin API** (used by the portal) - `POST /admin/hmac` — create a new entry (generate kid, set scope) - `DELETE /admin/hmac/{kid}` — retire an entry - Auth: OpenBao AppRole, or mTLS **Deployment topology** The topology depends on the environment. *Internet-facing deployments (aimer-web stack): two separate instances from v1* ```yaml # internal services responder — existing, untouched bootroot-http01-responder-internal: image: bootroot-http01-responder environment: - MODE=master - MASTER_HMAC_PATH=secret/bootroot/http01-hmac ports: ["80:80"] networks: [internal] # endpoint responder — new, separate instance for the aimer-web endpoints provisioner bootroot-http01-responder-endpoints: image: bootroot-http01-responder environment: - MODE=scoped - SCOPED_STORE_PATH=secret/endpoints/http01-hmac-store ports: ["80:80"] # behind a distinct DNS name / load balancer networks: [public] ``` The two processes share nothing: separate deploy, separate HMAC store, separate network namespace, separate monitoring. A compromise or bug in the endpoint responder cannot leak master HMAC material, and vice versa. *Closed-network deployments (aice-web-next stack): A-single is allowed* ```yaml bootroot-http01-responder: image: bootroot-http01-responder environment: - MODE=dual - MASTER_HMAC_PATH=secret/bootroot/http01-hmac - SCOPED_STORE_PATH=secret/endpoints/http01-hmac-store ports: ["80:80"] ``` Inside a closed network the internal services responder and the endpoint responder already share a trust zone (both are operated by the same customer admin). Running them as a single dual-mode process reduces operational complexity without widening the blast radius. **The operator may still opt for the two-instance topology** if audit or segmentation requirements demand it; the two choices are configuration-only and can be swapped without a code change. ### Summary of bootroot-side work (one prerequisite issue) - **Draft title**: "Extend bootroot-http01-responder with scoped HMAC mode for customer endpoints" - **Scope**: code extension, OpenBao KV schema additions, new admin API, documentation - **Testing**: regression of the existing master mode, the new scoped mode, scope-violation rejection, and concurrent use of both modes - **Organizational coordination**: requires a decision from the bootroot team, assuming agreement on Plan A+ - Can proceed **in parallel** with the main enrollment work; must be merged by the time integration testing begins --- ## Giganto / giganto-client prerequisite work ### Giganto repo — "Enforce host authorization — client cert SAN verification + deny list" **Scope** 1. **Cert SAN verification** (addresses A5) - Extract the SAN/CN from the peer cert during the QUIC handshake - Verify that every event's `agent_name` field in that connection matches the extracted identifier - On mismatch, drop the event (or reject the connection) and log 2. **Deny list** (addresses H3) - `HashSet` in memory with disk persistence (restored on restart) - Entries kept only until the cert's NotAfter, then removed - Check the cert serial after the QUIC handshake → **send a denial response and close** if it matches - Periodic (every minute) or event-driven sweep of active connections → send a denial response to matching connections and close them 3. **Explicit denial response** (addresses Layer 2) - Instead of a plain TCP/QUIC close, first send a giganto-client protocol **`HOST_DENIED` response message**, then close - This is what allows the agent to recognize the denial and transition to Suspended on its own - **Distinguish** deny-list rejection from SAN mismatch with different error codes so both the agent and the operator can see the cause 4. **Deny list GraphQL mutations and query** (on Giganto's existing mTLS-authenticated GraphQL endpoint) - `mutation addDenyListEntry(certSerial, expiresAt)` — add an entry - `mutation removeDenyListEntry(certSerial)` — remove early - `query denyList` — list entries 5. **Enrollment confirmation via GraphQL subscription** - New `sensorConnected` subscription on the existing GraphQL schema: emits `SensorConnectionEvent { agentName, certSerial, timestamp }` when a QUIC ingest connection arrives with a previously unseen cert serial for a given `agent_name` - New `connectedSensors` query: returns the current list of connected sensors with their cert serials, for portal catch-up after subscription reconnection - The portal subscribes over the existing mTLS-authenticated GraphQL WebSocket. No new outbound HTTP client is needed in Giganto - This triggers Phase 2 of the enrollment lifecycle on the portal side **Sub-decisions** - **SAN format**: `.endpoints.`, where `` is a ULID or UUID string - **agent_name ↔ SAN mapping**: `agent_name` in events contains just the ``, which must match the leftmost label of the cert SAN - **Error code naming**: `HOST_DENIED_REVOKED` (deny list) / `HOST_DENIED_SAN_MISMATCH` (SAN mismatch) and similar specific codes ### giganto-client repo — "Add HOST_DENIED response type for explicit agent rejection" giganto-client is a **binary protocol library** — it defines length-delimited bincode frames over QUIC streams, not HTTP/REST. `HOST_DENIED` is a new frame type in this binary protocol because it travels over the same QUIC connection that carries event data (reproduce ↔ Giganto). Note: the enrollment confirmation (Giganto → portal) uses a **GraphQL subscription** (`sensorConnected`) on Giganto's existing GraphQL schema, not this binary protocol. It lives entirely in the Giganto repo, not in giganto-client. See "Enrollment lifecycle: two-phase confirmation" above. **Scope** - Add a new frame/response type to the QUIC binary protocol: `HostDeniedResponse { reason: DeniedReason }` - `DeniedReason` enum: `Revoked`, `SanMismatch`, `AccountSuspended`, and similar variants - Sender-side (Giganto) serialization and receiver-side (`reproduce-*`) deserialization and handling - Maintain backwards compatibility with the existing protocol (new message type only, no changes to existing frame handling) **Dependency** - The Giganto work depends on this type, so giganto-client must be **merged and released first** - `reproduce-*`'s Layer 2 self-suspension implementation also consumes this type ### Independence Both issues are prerequisites for this work but can proceed **in parallel**. Both must be merged by integration-test time. --- ## Data governance Endpoint telemetry from Sysmon, Falco, and osquery routinely carries personal and sensitive data: user names, full file paths, command lines (which may contain secrets, URLs, search queries), process environments, open network connections, and more. Treating this as "just security logs" would expose the organization to unnecessary regulatory and customer-trust risk. Data governance is therefore a first-class part of this design, not an afterthought. The design addresses five concerns: minimization, redaction, retention, data-subject request handling, and region pinning. Each is scoped to what is realistically deliverable in v1; more advanced controls are noted as v2 candidates. ### Legal and regulatory framing Concrete obligations depend on where the data is collected and where it is stored: - **Korea PIPA**: minimization of collection (Art. 16), purpose limitation (Art. 18), safe handling (Art. 29), destruction after retention period (Art. 21), controls on cross-border transfer (Art. 28-8, 28-9). - **EU GDPR**: lawful basis (Art. 6), minimization and purpose limitation (Art. 5), data subject rights (Art. 15–22), DPIA when systematic monitoring of employees is involved (Art. 35), international transfer mechanisms (Chapter V). - **EU CRA**: technical documentation, support period, vulnerability handling, and risk assessment obligations for products placed on the EU market (effective 2024-12-10, full application 2027-12-11). - **California CCPA/CPRA**: employee data has been in scope since the 2023-01-01 expiry of the employee exemption. - **United States (sectoral)**: HIPAA if any covered health data is captured; GLBA for financial institutions. This design does not attempt to be "PIPA-compliant" or "GDPR-compliant" on its own — compliance is determined by the full deployment context. What it does is provide the technical primitives that a compliant deployment requires: a place to apply minimization, a hook to apply redaction, a knob to set retention, and a path for data-subject requests to reach the data. ### 1. Field minimization (v1 required) Not every Sysmon/Falco/osquery field is sent to Giganto. A per-kind **field allowlist** is maintained in the `reproduce` repo under `configs/field-allowlists/`, one file per `RawEventKind`. Fields not on the allowlist are dropped by the Collector *before* serialization, so they never leave the host. Examples of fields that are explicitly **not** on the default allowlist: - Sysmon `CommandLine` full text (only the executable path is on the list; the full command-line becomes opt-in via `kind: sysmon_full_cmdline`) - Sysmon `User` raw principal name (only a hashed form) - Falco `proc.cmdline`, `fd.name` for user-space paths under `/home` - osquery `processes.cmdline`, `process_open_files.path` under user home directories The allowlist is versioned alongside the code, reviewed by the security team on every change, and shipped as part of the `reproduce-*` binary. Changing the allowlist is a code change, not a runtime config change, so customer operators cannot silently widen the scope. ### 2. Per-tenant redaction (v2 — deferred) In v1, field minimization is handled entirely at the agent side (see §1 above). Giganto receives only the fields that passed the agent-side allowlist and stores them as-is. No Giganto-side redaction is applied. In v2, customers will be able to configure additional redaction rules per tenant (regex masking, allowlist overrides, path shortening) via an `ingest_policy` table managed by the portal and pushed to Giganto. Redaction would be applied at Giganto ingest time, enabling per-customer rules that evolve independently of agent releases. This is deferred to v2 because it requires Giganto to gain per-tenant awareness in its storage layer — a significant structural change to a system that currently stores all events in a shared RocksDB with a single global retention policy. ### 3. Retention (v1 — Giganto's existing global retention; per-tenant retention in v2) Giganto already has a global retention mechanism (`retain_periodically()`, default 100 days, configurable per deployment). In v1, this existing mechanism is used as-is — all events share the same retention period regardless of tenant. Per-tenant retention (different TTLs per customer or environment) is deferred to v2 because Giganto's current RocksDB storage is not partitioned by tenant. Adding per-tenant retention requires either per-tenant column families, a tenant-aware key prefix scheme, or a secondary index — all of which are significant storage-layer changes. For v1 compliance purposes, the global retention period should be set to the **shortest** required by any tenant's policy. Customer DPAs should document the global retention value. ### 4. Data-subject requests (v2 — deferred) PIPA and GDPR both require that individuals can request access to, correction of, or deletion of data about them. Because endpoint telemetry is attributed to *hosts*, not *users*, honoring such a request requires tracing from a user identifier through the events that reference it, which in turn requires Giganto to support per-field querying and targeted deletion — capabilities it does not have today. DSR execution is deferred to v2 in its entirety. When implemented, the design will include: - Exact-match-only search on a whitelisted set of identifier fields - Two-stage workflow with preview before execution - Hard delete by default (GDPR Art. 17 "without undue delay", PIPA Art. 21 "without delay"); quarantine only with an explicit legal-hold override - Export auditing with signed archives - Per-tenant job tracking For v1, the agent-side field allowlist (§1) serves as the primary mitigation: fields most likely to carry personal data (`command_line`, `user`, paths under `/home/`) can be excluded from collection entirely, so that DSR requests against those fields have no matching data in Giganto. If a DSR request arises before v2 is ready, the operator must handle it manually using Giganto's existing data export and RocksDB-level tooling. ### 5. Region pinning and cross-border transfer (v1 required for aimer-web) aimer-web is internet-facing and may collect data from customers in jurisdictions that restrict cross-border transfer (EU, Korea, China, etc.). Each aimer-web Environment has a **region** attribute (`environment.region`), which determines: - Which Giganto instance receives the events (regional Giganto deployment). - Which step-ca instance signs the certificates (regional CA). - Which `bootroot-http01-responder` instance handles the ACME validation. v1 ships with at least one region; additional regions are deployed as customer demand requires. An Environment cannot move across regions without a full re-enrollment of its hosts (consistent with the "portal binding is permanent" principle). aice-web-next is closed-network and all infrastructure lives inside the customer's own environment, so cross-border transfer does not apply by construction — the customer's own PIPA/GDPR obligations determine the placement. #### Metadata centralization — explicit acknowledgement Region pinning above only covers the **event data path** (Sysmon/Falco/osquery telemetry → Giganto). The **portal metadata path** is handled separately and currently centralized: - The portal database (aice-web-next or aimer-web) holds host UUIDs, host display names, customer- or admin-supplied descriptions, audit trails of admin actions, activation token issuance records, DSR job records, and observed/expected fingerprints. - This metadata is **itself personal data** in many jurisdictions: a host display name and an admin description routinely identify a specific employee or device. - In v1, aimer-web's portal database is **centralized**, not regionalized. That means metadata for an EU-region or Korea-region Environment may be stored on infrastructure outside that region. This is a deliberate v1 trade-off, not an oversight. v1 mitigates the risk in three ways: 1. **Field minimization at the portal level.** The portal restricts free-text fields: `host.description` is capped at a short length, and the UI guidance steers admins away from putting personal names in it. The host display name field is similarly restricted. Customer-supplied free text is the smallest possible footprint. 2. **Audit log scrubbing.** Audit log entries record actor account IDs (opaque UUIDs), not personal names, wherever possible. Where a personal name leaks in (for example an admin's display name), the audit row carries it; this is acceptable because admin identities are inside the operating organization, not the customer's data subjects. 3. **Contractual disclosure.** Customer Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) must explicitly state that portal metadata is centralized in the operator's region, list which fields cross borders, and identify the basis for transfer (SCCs, adequacy, etc.). This is a customer-contract obligation that goes hand in hand with the technical setup. A **regional portal database shard** — splitting the portal database itself by region so that metadata for an EU customer never leaves the EU — is a v2 candidate. It is not in v1 because it requires the portal application to become region-aware throughout (login routing, audit aggregation, cross-shard queries), which is a much larger change than the host-authorization scope of this work. aice-web-next is not affected: it runs entirely inside the customer's closed network, so its portal metadata never leaves that network in the first place. ### 6. Audit, DPIA, and customer-facing documentation - **Audit logging (v1)** — changes to the agent-side field allowlist configuration are tracked via code review (the allowlist is versioned in the reproduce repo). In v2, when Giganto gains per-tenant `ingest_policy`, every change to an `ingest_policy` row will be logged in `audit_db` with actor, timestamp, and before/after values. - **DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment)** — deployments that involve systematic monitoring of employees must run a DPIA under GDPR Art. 35. This design does not conduct the DPIA; it provides the documentation, data flows, and configuration surface that the DPIA requires as input. - **Customer-facing privacy documentation** — the default field allowlist and the global retention period are published in customer documentation so that customers can include them in their own privacy notices. Per-tenant redaction capabilities will be documented when available in v2. ### v2 / out of scope - **Giganto per-tenant data governance engine** — per-tenant redaction at ingest time, per-tenant retention TTL, DSR execution engine (search, delete, export). Requires Giganto to gain tenant-aware storage (currently single shared RocksDB with global retention). This is the single largest v2 item. - **Pseudonymization of user identifiers** at ingest (stable hash + separate lookup table) — defers to v2 because it affects detection-rule authoring. - **Field-level encryption at rest** per tenant — v2. - **Automatic detection of new sensitive fields** in future Sysmon/Falco/osquery versions — v2. ### Scope boundary restated This section defines *what reproduce-\* and the portals will do*. It does not: - Determine whether any specific deployment is legally compliant (that is the customer's obligation with their own DPO/legal counsel). - Replace the need for a DPIA or a PIPA privacy impact assessment in the deployments that require them. - Cover contractual issues (data processing agreements, sub-processor lists, customer contracts). What it does guarantee is that the **foundational compliance primitive** is present from v1: **agent-side field minimization** (data that is never collected cannot be a compliance liability) plus Giganto's existing global retention. Per-tenant redaction, per-tenant retention, and DSR execution are v2 items that build on top of this foundation once Giganto gains tenant-aware storage. Region pinning of event data is v1 for aimer-web deployments. --- ## Platform-specific `reproduce-*` implementation ### Common structure Structure shared by all three binaries: - All of them reuse the common-library traits (`EnrollmentClient`, `KeyStore`, `Controller`, `AgentState`). - Each `main.rs` is a thin layer that assembles `load config → initialize KeyStore → run Enrollment (or load existing Identity) → Controller::run`. - Service-manager integration lives in a per-OS adapter (`service.rs`, `systemd.rs`, `launchd.rs`). - Log sinks are per-OS (`tracing-eventlog`, `tracing-journald`, or an `os_log` wrapper). ### reproduce-windows - **Collection**: Sysmon (Operational channel) — EventLogCollector (#797 Phase 3) - **Service**: Windows Service Control Manager (`windows-service` crate) - **Logs**: Windows Event Log (`tracing-eventlog` or ETW) - **Packaging**: MSI via WiX v4 - **Signing**: SSL.com EV + eSigner - **Host fingerprint**: `HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography\MachineGuid` - **Key storage**: two backends available from v1 — `WindowsCertStore` (LocalMachine\\My, preferred for production) and PEM files with service-account-only ACL (`icacls`, used when the Cert Store is not available). The choice is a service configuration option; both backends implement the common `KeyStore` trait - **Sysmon bundle**: the MSI ships Sysmon64.exe + sysmon-config.xml with SHA256 verification ### reproduce-linux (Debian 12 / Ubuntu 22.04 LTS / Ubuntu 24.04 LTS) - **Collection**: Falco (modern eBPF driver by default). osquery added in a follow-up phase - **Service**: systemd **system service**. `Type=notify`, `Restart=on-failure` - **Logs**: journald (`tracing-journald`) - **Packaging**: a single `.deb` (amd64) - **Signing**: GPG-signed apt repo (new infrastructure to be built) - **Host fingerprint**: `/etc/machine-id` - **Key storage**: PEM with mode 0600 and a dedicated `reproduce` user - **Build environment**: Ubuntu 22.04 container (the oldest supported glibc target) - **CI**: a single build followed by smoke tests across all three distributions ### reproduce-macos - **Collection**: osquery (installed separately or bundled in the pkg) - **Service**: launchd LaunchDaemon (system-wide) - **Logs**: Unified Log (`os_log` wrapper, or stdio → launchd) - **Packaging**: `.pkg` via productbuild - **Signing**: Apple Developer ID Application + notarization (`notarytool`) - **Host fingerprint**: `IOPlatformUUID` (via `IOKit`) - **Key storage**: PEM with mode 0600, owned by `root:wheel`. Keychain option considered in v2 - **osquery integration**: install osqueryd as a LaunchDaemon → tail the results log (`osqueryd.results.log`) → parse → convert to Giganto format → send - **v2 candidate**: Endpoint Security framework collector. Requires the `com.apple.developer.endpoint-security.client` entitlement (tracked separately) ### Platform-independence check The common library must provide all of the following in a platform-independent manner: | Component | Windows | Linux | macOS | |---|---|---|---| | EnrollmentClient | ✓ common | ✓ common | ✓ common | | KeyStore (PEM v1) | ✓ common + ACL adapter | ✓ common + 0600 adapter | ✓ common + 0600 adapter | | AgentState machine | ✓ common | ✓ common | ✓ common | | HostIdentity | MachineGuid | /etc/machine-id | IOPlatformUUID | | Collector | EventLogCollector | FalcoCollector / OsqueryCollector | OsqueryCollector | | Service adapter | SCM | systemd sd_notify | launchd | | Log sink | tracing-eventlog | tracing-journald | os_log | | Packaging | MSI (WiX) | deb | pkg | | Code signing | Authenticode | GPG (repo) | Developer ID + notarization | --- ## Phase plan (extending #797) - **Phase 1** ✅ (#812) — `[lib] + [[bin]]` layout, parser relocation, sender extraction, `Checkpoint` - **Phase 2** ✅ (#813) — controller/collector commonization, `run_pipeline()`, existing reproduce structural cleanup - **Phase 3** (planned, #797) — `[[bin]] reproduce-windows` + `[[bin]] reproduce-linux` scaffolds, initial EventLogCollector, Falco integration begins - **Phase 4a — Common library + Linux reference** (this work, split into four sub-phases for incremental review) - **Phase 4a-1 — Foundations** - `config.rs` schema migration: accept hostname-based URLs for step-ca, responder, and Giganto (currently `SocketAddr` only; see [src/config.rs](https://github.com/aicers/reproduce/blob/main/src/config.rs)) - New `src/lib.rs` modules: `keystore/` (trait + PemFileStore), `host/` (HostIdentity trait + Linux implementation), `enrollment/bundle.rs` (ActivationBundle parsing + validation) - Portal-side initial host-table schema migration (aice-web-next + aimer-web), including the trust-model columns - **Phase 4a-2 — Enrollment client** - `src/enrollment/acme.rs` with `instant-acme` (initial enrollment only, no renewal yet) - `src/enrollment/responder_client.rs` for HTTP-01 token registration with scoped HMAC - Portal authorization webhook endpoint (`POST /api/authz/host`) - bootroot responder scoped HMAC mode extension (can land in parallel) - **Phase 4a-3 — State machine + renewal + denial handling** - `src/agent_state/` state machine with the full transition table - Renewal loop with authoritative denial handling (`EnrollmentError::Denied`) - giganto-client `HOST_DENIED` response type (can land in parallel) - Giganto deny list + `HOST_DENIED` emission (can land in parallel) - Layer 2 agent self-suspension integration - **Phase 4a-4 — Linux integration + cross-repo conformance** - reproduce-linux end-to-end: systemd adapter, FalcoCollector, `/etc/machine-id` HostIdentity - End-to-end integration tests: reproduce-linux + portal + step-ca + Giganto + deny list + self-suspension + enrollment confirmation - **Cross-repo conformance test suite**: shared test fixtures that exercise the contract boundaries between repos — webhook JSON payloads, `HOST_DENIED` wire format, `activation.json` schema, enrollment confirmation notification, CSR OID extensions. These run in CI for each repo that implements a side of the contract, using the shared fixtures as golden files. This catches drift between prose/spec and code before it reaches production - Data governance v1: **agent-side field allowlist loader** (`configs/field-allowlists/` → Collector drops non-allowed fields before serialization). Giganto-side ingest-time redaction and per-tenant retention are v2 - **Phase 4b — Windows platform-specific work (in parallel with 4a)** - Complete EventLogCollector - Windows Service adapter (SCM) - Windows Event Log tracing sink - Windows host fingerprint, ACL-based key storage - MSI (WiX v4) project, activation bundle input UI, Sysmon bundle - CI build (unsigned) - **Phase 5 — Windows integration** - After the Phase 4a common library stabilizes, combine with reproduce-windows - End-to-end verification in an internal test environment using the unsigned MSI - **Phase 6 — Windows production signing + pilot** - SSL.com EV certificate and eSigner integration (CI) - Signed MSI distribution - Initial customer pilot - **Phase 7 — macOS port** - reproduce-macos scaffold - OsqueryCollector (reusing the one built in Phase 4) - launchd adapter, pkg packaging, notarization pipeline - Apple Developer Program registration (prerequisite work) - **Phase 8 — Linux osquery addition** - Add OsqueryCollector alongside Phase 3's Falco collector - reproduce-linux gains the ability to pick Falco or osquery --- ## Prerequisite work (external dependencies) These are the prerequisites for starting Phase 4. Every item runs **in parallel**, and given the lead times involved, all of them should be started within the organization immediately. ### Organizational and procurement tasks (start in parallel) 1. **Obtain a D-U-N-S number** — apply through Korean Dun & Bradstreet. This is a **prerequisite for both the Windows EV certificate and the macOS Apple Developer Program**, and must be started first. 2. **Request SSL.com EV + eSigner** — starts once the D-U-N-S number is in hand. Two to three weeks to issuance. 3. **Apple Developer Program (Organization enrollment)** — starts once the D-U-N-S number is in hand. One to four weeks to approval. 4. **Build the Linux deb signing infrastructure from scratch** — GPG key creation, repo hosting, and a CI signing pipeline. Not urgent; can proceed in parallel after the Windows work begins. 5. **Coordinate with the bootroot team** — secure organizational agreement on the scoped HMAC mode extension and its delivery schedule. ### Separate prerequisite issues (one per repo) 6. **bootroot#N** — add a scoped HMAC mode to the responder (Plan A+). 7. **giganto-client#N** — add the `HOST_DENIED` response type. Must be merged before the Giganto work, since Giganto depends on the type. 8. **giganto#N** — host authorization enforcement (SAN verification, deny list, admin API, and sending `HOST_DENIED`). 9. **aice-web-next#N** — host authorization data model, API, and UI. 10. **aimer-web#N** — host authorization (two-tier allocation) data model, API, and UI. Once agreement is reached, each of these will be tracked as a **stub discussion** in its respective repo — linking back here and summarizing the scope for that repo — and then split into implementation issues. --- ## Open questions All design-level decisions have been settled. What remains are details that will be resolved naturally during implementation. - **Responder domain naming** — the actual `*.endpoints.` DNS zones for closed-network and internet environments are an operator decision. - **Rust ACME client choice** — `instant-acme` is the leading candidate (pending verification of its EAB support); to be finalized when implementation begins. - **Per-host HMAC kid format** — whether to use a ULID with a prefix or a different scheme is an implementation detail. - **Cert lifetime tuning** — the v1 default is 24 hours, but it can be adjusted to 12h, 48h, or 72h based on operational experience. ### v2 candidates (out of scope, future decisions) - **Hardware-rooted device identity (`device-attest-01` + TPM / Secure Enclave)** — replaces the Path A "stable hardware identifier" approach with cryptographic attestation. Requires that step-ca's open-source `device-attest-01` flow becomes end-to-end usable, and that TPM 2.0 / Secure Enclave is available on the target hosts. Where available, this elevates Path A from "raises the bar" to "cryptographically rooted" and is the proper long-term answer to the bundle-theft threat model. - **macOS Endpoint Security framework collector** — requires entitlement application and a System Extension implementation. - **Linux / macOS native key backends** — kernel keyring, macOS Keychain. Windows Cert Store ships in v1; the others follow. - **Staged CA trust for zero-downtime CA rotation** — Giganto trusts both the old and the new root during a migration window so that a fleet can rotate its CA without per-host reinstall. See "Portal binding is permanent" for context. - **Signed authorization lease for offline renewal** — the portal pre-issues a short-lived signed token (e.g. a JWT with the host's authorization state, valid for N hours) that step-ca can validate locally without calling the webhook. This would allow cert renewals to proceed during brief portal outages, removing the hard portal dependency for renewals noted in the "Partial independence from portal availability" section. - **Advanced data-subject-request workflow** — self-service request intake, automated 30-day deadline tracking, region-scoped execution. - **Pseudonymization at ingest** — stable hash of user identifiers with a separate lookup table. - **Field-level encryption at rest per tenant**. - **Regional portal database shards** — splits the portal metadata store by region so that metadata for an EU or Korea customer never leaves its region. Requires the portal application (login routing, audit aggregation, cross-shard queries) to become region-aware. Pairs with the v1 region-pinning of event data described in "Data governance §5". - **A-double topology for closed-network deployments** — closed-network operators who want audit-level segmentation can move to the same two-instance topology used by internet-facing deployments. - **CRL or OCSP** — only needed if additional cert verifiers appear alongside Giganto. - **Air-gapped deployment** — an offline enrollment protocol plus manual bundle delivery. --- ## References ### Prior discussions / issues - aicers/reproduce#797 — reproduce restructuring + reproduce-windows implementation plan (the source for this work) - aicers/reproduce#812 — Phase 1: `[lib] + [[bin]]` restructuring ✅ - aicers/reproduce#813 — Phase 2: controller/collector commonization ✅ ### External documents - bootroot `ARCHITECTURE.md` — the PKI foundation for this work: - [§5 System Authentication Model](https://github.com/aicers/bootroot/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md#5-system-authentication-model) — the existing table of mTLS connections inside the organization; `reproduce-* → Giganto (mTLS)` is the new row this work adds - [§6.2 Environment Separation](https://github.com/aicers/bootroot/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md#62-environment-separation) — closed-network vs internet CA split, trust roots never shared - [§7.1 ACME as the Primary Mechanism](https://github.com/aicers/bootroot/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md#71-acme-as-the-primary-mechanism) — ACME as the standard issuance protocol - [§8 Certificate Lifetime and Rotation](https://github.com/aicers/bootroot/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md#8-certificate-lifetime-and-rotation) — short-lived certs and automatic rotation - [bootroot `DESIGN.md`](https://github.com/aicers/bootroot/blob/main/DESIGN.md) — certificate rotation, secret management, automation boundaries - aice-web-next `decisions/account-management.md` — customer / role / customer_db structure - aimer-web `docs/en/environment-management.md` — Environment and Trust Registry - Smallstep official docs: - https://smallstep.com/docs/step-ca/acme-basics/ - https://smallstep.com/docs/step-ca/provisioners/ - https://smallstep.com/blog/acme-eab-overview/ - [smallstep/certificates#650 — ACME External Account Binding (merged 2022-01-31)](https://github.com/smallstep/certificates/pull/650) ### External crate candidates - `instant-acme` — Rust ACME client - `windows-service` — Windows Service integration - `rcgen` — CSR generation - `rustls`, `quinn` — mTLS (already in use) - `tracing-eventlog`, `tracing-journald` — per-platform log sinks --- ## The role of this discussion This discussion is the **canonical source for rationale and design decisions**. It is intentionally *not* the canonical source for interface contracts. The distinction matters: | Artifact | Lives in | Versioned how | Example | |---|---|---|---| | Rationale, trade-offs, accepted decisions | This discussion (#846) | Prose, with edit history | "We chose HTTP-01 + bootroot responder because…" | | **Interface contracts** | **Spec files in each affected repo**, committed alongside the implementing code | Semver, with review | `activation.json` schema, `HOST_DENIED` wire format, authorization webhook JSON | Concretely, each of the following will have a versioned spec file in its home repo once the interface is ready to implement: - `reproduce/specs/activation-bundle.md` — `activation.json` schema, TTL, trust model references - `reproduce/specs/agent-state.md` — the state machine transitions and the events that drive them - `giganto-client/specs/host-denied.md` — `HOST_DENIED` message layout, reason codes - `giganto/specs/deny-list.md` — deny list GraphQL mutations, query, and storage semantics - `giganto/specs/enrollment-confirmation.md` — `sensorConnected` subscription schema and `connectedSensors` query for Phase 2 enrollment confirmation - `aice-web-next/specs/authz-webhook.md` and `aimer-web/specs/authz-webhook.md` — the step-ca authorizing webhook contract, identical between the two portals - `bootroot/specs/scoped-hmac.md` — the scoped HMAC registration API Changes to a spec file require a code review in its own repo and a reference back to an updated section of this discussion if the rationale has changed. This keeps discussion prose from becoming the single point of failure for cross-repo compatibility. Once the design is agreed, work proceeds as follows: 1. Finalize this discussion as the agreed version of the rationale. 2. Register stub discussions or issues in each repo (bootroot, giganto, giganto-client, aice-web-next, aimer-web), each linking back here. 3. Draft the initial spec files in each repo as part of Phase 4a-1. 4. Finalize repo-specific details through reviews with the relevant owners. 5. Start the organizational prerequisites in parallel (D-U-N-S, SSL.com EV, Apple Developer Program, Linux deb infrastructure). 6. In the reproduce repo, begin Phase 4a-1 through 4a-4 followed by 4b once Phase 3 is complete. 7. This discussion lives on as a link hub — rationale here, contracts in the spec files, code in the implementing PRs. Review and feedback are welcome. In particular, we'd like input on: - **Cross-portal schema compatibility** — whether the API contract of the two-tier allocation model stays aligned between aice-web-next and aimer-web. - **bootroot responder scoped HMAC mode extension** — whether the bootroot team can accept this direction, and any alternatives worth considering. - **Giganto host authorization enforcement** — the SAN format, the deny list lifetime policy, and the details of the `HOST_DENIED` protocol. - **Phase 4a/4b parallelism** — how to reach early agreement on the trait signatures needed to unblock the Windows track while the Linux reference is still in flight.

nodes.title: Python + AI Weekly Office Hours: Recordings & Resources
nodes.body:
Each week, we hold weekly office hours about all things Python + AI in the Foundry Discord.
Join the Discord here: http://aka.ms/aipython/oh

This thread will list the recordings of each office hours, and any other resources that come out of the OH sessions. The questions and answers are automatically posted (based on the transcript) as comments in this thread.

# Nov 10, 2026

* [Recording](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LvVH3W4-xpg)

Topics covered:

* [Announcement: Skills over MCP arrives in the GitHub Copilot harness](#discussioncomment-19549432)
* [Announcement: Azure OpenAI starter kit adds Decisions API samples](#discussioncomment-19549433)
* [Announcement: Claude adds message threads](#discussioncomment-19549434)
* [Announcement: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Cyber](#discussioncomment-19549435)
* [Announcement: AI coding startups consolidate](#discussioncomment-19549436)
* [Discussion: Security breaches and technology in healthcare](#discussioncomment-19549437)
* [Discussion: The impact of AI on the CS curriculum](#discussioncomment-19549438)
* [Announcement: GitHub and Azure updates](#discussioncomment-19549439)
* [Demo: GitHub in Slack and Teams](#discussioncomment-19549440)
* [Announcement: Python 3.10 is end of life](#discussioncomment-19549441)
* [Announcement: Image and video models across the industry](#discussioncomment-19549443)
* [Announcement: Latest research into agent reasoning and hallucinations](#discussioncomment-19549445)
* [If an agent can only access what the asking user can access, how can Microsoft IQ use a company-wide knowledge graph to give good answers?](#discussioncomment-19549446)
